text:
Image-only reading of packet 05

Orientation and layout
All six supplied images were successfully viewed. Images 001 and 002 are overall views of the two exposed surfaces; 003-004 enlarge the surface in 001, and 005-006 enlarge the surface in 002. The musical writing is upright as displayed, with horizontal red staves and text below. The later cursive writing in the middle of 001/003 is differently oriented and is not treated as chant text. The ruler and color target are photographic apparatus.

The more complete surviving systems have FIVE red horizontal lines. Double vertical red ruling occurs at the left. Dark notation includes lozenge-like heads and connected or elongated shapes. The peeled and folded material hides much of each system. I cannot securely identify a clef and its line. In particular, the tall dark shapes at the left of some exposed systems could be clefs or parts of compound notes; they should not be converted automatically into sung notes. No absolute pitch is assigned.

Relative positions below use an upward diatonic staff step as +1. An adjacent line and space differ by one. Each independently bounded passage starts at 0. These are short local observations, not a reconstructed melody.

Passage A: image 004, lower left, about 24%-31% across and 47%-56% down; also visible near the lower left of image 001.
Two relatively clear lozenge heads lie in the same space between the second and third staff lines counted from the top: [0, 0]. Before these, near the left red vertical ruling, is a taller pale mark spanning more than one height. I cannot securely determine whether it is a clef, a multi-note shape, or damaged ink. I exclude it from the sequence. The right-hand continuation disappears beneath a substantial raised fold. After collapsing repeats this gives only one securely read pitch position.

Passage B: image 004, lower central-right exposed staff, approximately 58%-63% across and 57%-65% down; also visible at the bottom center of image 001.
The final two clear lozenges before the exposed area ends descend one staff step: [0, -1]. The first is centered on the fourth line from the top, the second in the space below it. This is a local two-note reading. To their left, a separate lozenge appears in the space above the fourth line; farther left another appears on approximately the third line. Taken merely as spatially visible heads, these suggest four descending levels, provisionally [0, -1, -2, -3]. HOWEVER, peeling/vertical missing strips interrupt the area between the earlier heads. I cannot establish that these are four consecutive sung notes with none lost, so that four-number pattern is not a reliable continuous melodic run. Do not bridge those gaps for comparison. The two rightmost heads appear to be ordinary notes within a broken system; there is no secure intact line-ending context for calling the last one a custos.

Passage C: image 005, upper-left staff, approximately 18%-23% across and 22%-28% down; also image 002 upper left.
Two pale but recognizable heads occupy the same space between the fourth and fifth lines: [0, 0]. The surrounding staff area is abraded and the continuation to the right is covered. There is no reliable longer sequence. The earlier left area does not yield a secure clef.

Passage D: image 005, second staff at left, approximately 14%-17% across and 58%-68% down.
A diagonal compound mark appears to descend from near the third line to the fourth line. If only its two endpoint heads are counted, their relative heights are approximately [0, -2]. There may be an intervening element at -1, but I cannot distinguish a separate head confidently from the connecting stroke and abrasion. Thus [0, -1?, -2] is an explicitly uncertain description of the shape, not a three-note transcription. Faint ink farther right is insufficient to continue the run.

Other surviving music
Image 003 contains isolated heads or compound dark shapes on the small central/right staff islands and at the bottom left. Missing surface and crop edges prevent a secure longer run. Image 006 shows very faint isolated marks on the left staves and a small central island of red ruling. Its dark central blotches do not support an unambiguous sequence of noteheads. Neither image supplies a reliable clef or an intact terminal sign identifiable as a custos. I do not interpret brown stains, peeled edges, or later pen strokes as notes.

Literal accompanying words
- Image 005, beneath the upper-left staff: "gaudio" is the clearest continuous word; the initial shape is somewhat faded.
- Image 005, below the next left staff: "it ... te" is a tentative literal reading of the exposed letters. Missing or damaged material prevents a phrase reading.
- Image 006, beneath the upper left exposed system: approximately "ch[?] ... vi[?]". I cannot securely resolve the middle letters and do not complete a word from expectation.
- Image 006, below its lower-left staff: approximately "[t/f]ron[...]", highly uncertain.
- Image 004, text under the central lower staff: only a fragment resembling "...ion..." is visible, with uncertain letters.
These readings concern the larger formal lettering associated with the music. I have not used the differently oriented later cursive annotations to infer musical text or identity.

Coverage and limitations
Viewed images 001, 002, 003, 004, 005, and 006, including every supplied enlarged crop. The obstacle is not simply small image size: the actual exposed music is divided into tiny islands by missing surface, blank coverings, folds, and abrasion. I can report several one- or two-position local observations and an uncertain descending shape. I do NOT find a reliable continuous run retaining at least four notes after adjacent repetitions collapse. The attractive four-level descent in image 004 is interrupted by physical damage and must not be promoted into a continuous four-note reading. No six-to-fourteen-note melody, absolute pitch sequence, or identity can responsibly be supplied from this viewing.
